title: 6 Practical AI Tips for Teachers
author: Paul Matthews
summary: Matthews argues that the wide gap between teachers who get real value from AI and teachers who get almost nothing is not a gap in tools but a gap in habits, since two colleagues at adjacent desks in the same staffroom have access to the same models. He offers six low-tech habits and insists throughout that the teacher, not the model, holds the authority: ask for fifteen multiple-choice questions and keep the best ten rather than accepting the first answer. The core distinction he draws is between tasks and jobs, with AI treated as a capable apprentice that can produce a hook or an exit ticket but cannot plan a whole lesson worth teaching. He warns about what he calls chat rot, where a single long-running conversation exceeds the context window and quietly forgets the instructions it was given, and recommends starting a fresh chat for each new task. He also pushes readers toward platform personalisation settings, speech to text rather than typing or voice mode, and a pre-mortem prompt that asks a model to explain why an idea has already failed. The piece closes by naming the point of the exercise: six better habits rather than six better tools, with the teacher still in the driver's seat.
points: The task-versus-job distinction is the operational heart of the piece, with a worked breakdown of a lesson into hook, direct instruction, stimulus, gradual-release activity, retrieval quiz and exit ticket.
Matthews names chat rot as a specific failure mode and ties it to the context window, recommending a new chat per task and comparing a chat to a workbench rather than a filing cabinet.
He gives concrete personalisation setup paths for ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot, including the character limits and the warning that a school tenant admin may have switched the feature off entirely.
The pre-mortem prompt is reproduced in full, with instructions to name unnoticed assumptions and expected objections and to withhold encouragement.
He rejects voice mode in favour of speech to text, on the grounds that talking is faster than typing and reading is faster than listening.
quotes: The big difference between good and bad AI users isn’t in the tech they use but the habits they adopt.
And, lest you be intimidated by this technology, remember that AI has never shaken a hand, spoken with a student, or taught a class.
As teachers, we have wisdom, experience, understanding, intuition, and pastoral knowledge that the AI will never have.
AI is a great apprentice but a terrible craftsman. We should check its work every step of the way.
If you are using a free version of ChatGPT or Claude then you have a few tens of thousands of words worth of context before it starts to forget prior parts of your conversation.
An AI chat is like a workbench, not a filing cabinet. Clear it between jobs.
The reason is simple - talking is faster than typing and reading is faster than listening.
And notice something - these aren’t six better tools. They’re six better habits that leave you - the human - firmly in the driver’s seat.
